title: Ankara Seeks Interpol Red Notice for Netanyahu Over Gaza Flotilla; Israel Hits Back With 'Antisemitic Dictator' Broadside
subhead: Turkey escalated its legal campaign against Israel by requesting an Interpol red notice for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over the May Gaza flotilla interception, drawing a blistering response from Netanyahu's office that widened the Ankara-Jerusalem rupture into Syria and Cyprus.

sections.heading: Turkey Requests Interpol Red Notice for Netanyahu
sections.body: Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said Friday that Ankara had asked the interior ministry to issue Interpol red notices for the arrest of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and another Israeli, named as Afek Moskovitch, as part of a domestic criminal case over the interception of the Global Sumud Flotilla in international waters in May, according to France 24 and Reuters. Gurlek said arrest warrants had been issued on charges including genocide, crimes against humanity and torture in a case against 35 people. Turkey's IHA news agency reported Moskovitch is an Israeli soldier accused over actions in Gaza, including posting footage of destruction at the Islamic University of Gaza. The flotilla, of about 50 vessels that left Turkey for Gaza, was detained by Israeli forces; activists alleged physical and sexual abuse during detention, and France, Italy and Australia have opened their own judicial proceedings.
sections.whyItMatters: A red notice is a request to police worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, so this moves Turkey's Gaza case from a domestic warrant to an international mechanism — though Interpol reviews and can decline such requests. It is the sharpest legal escalation yet in Ankara's campaign to hold Israeli leaders accountable.

sections.heading: Netanyahu's Office Fires Back, Widening the Rupture
sections.body: Netanyahu's office dismissed the move as a 'pathetic attempt to intimidate' Israeli leaders and soldiers, and repeated a blistering characterization of Erdogan as an 'antisemitic dictator who has massacred Kurds, harbors Hamas terrorists, occupies half of Cyprus, and jails record numbers of journalists and politicians who oppose him', per TASS and Greek City Times. The statement added that Erdogan 'now seeks to extend his aggression against Israel into Syria' and that 'Israel will not tolerate it.' Ankara's presidential office in turn denounced Netanyahu's 'petty political tactics' and slammed the Israeli government's attempt 'to present Turkey as a new threat,' according to France 24. Ankara has suggested Israeli rhetoric is fueled by the approach of Israel's parliamentary election in October.
sections.whyItMatters: The exchange shows the Turkey-Israel rupture has moved beyond policy disagreement into a personal, escalating war of words that now explicitly links Syria, Cyprus and the Kurds — a sign both governments see political value in the confrontation, with Israeli elections approaching.

sections.heading: NATO Article 5 Debate Sharpens Over Syria
sections.body: An Israeli strategic expert, Shay Gal of Line of State, argued in Israel Hayom that Turkey's NATO membership does not automatically protect its servicemen in Syria, writing that Article 5 'protects Turkish territory; Turkish troops do not carry that territory with them onto Syrian or occupied Cypriot soil,' and that NATO acts by consensus, per TASS. Gal described Israel's apparent doctrine as to 'deny infrastructure before the flag lands' — striking the Abu al-Duhur air base before Turkish forces could arrive and entrench. Separately, a bankingnews.gr report cited Israeli deliberations over striking Turkish assets beyond borders to bypass NATO Article 5, with Cyprus described as 'the weak link in an Israeli-Turkish dispute.'
sections.whyItMatters: The debate over whether Article 5 covers Turkish forces outside Turkish territory is central to how far Israel can go. It signals that Israeli planners are actively gaming out scenarios that could involve Turkish assets in Syria, the Mediterranean or Cyprus — a significant escalation in strategic thinking.

sections.heading: Syria Courts Pakistan, Defends Turkey's Role
sections.body: Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al-Shaibani made the first visit by a Syrian foreign minister to Pakistan in nearly two decades, where he said Damascus was considering whether to join or cooperate with the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement signed this month by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, according to the Express Tribune. Shaibani strongly defended Ankara, saying 'Turkey has stood with Syria and its people over the past 14 years and is an important ally' and that 'Israel has no right to tell us who our ally or partner can be.' He also indicated Damascus would not object to Pakistani mediation with Iran under certain conditions. No decision was reached on joining the grouping.
sections.whyItMatters: Syria's outreach to Pakistan — a nuclear-armed member of the new Makkah pact — signals Damascus is seeking leverage against Israel after the Abu al-Duhur strike, while publicly anchoring itself to the Turkey-Saudi-Pakistan axis. It also shows the Makkah pact is being positioned as a broader Islamic security umbrella.

sections.heading: Somalia Clarifies It Has Not Recognized Northern Cyprus
sections.body: Somalia's foreign ministry on Friday denied having recognized northern Cyprus as an independent state, after new Parliament Speaker Abdulkadir Mohamed Nur posted a now-deleted message thanking the north's 'parliament speaker' Ziya Ozturkler for congratulating him on his August 10 election, per Cyprus Mail. The ministry said the post was 'personal communication' that does not reflect a change in foreign policy and reaffirmed respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Republic of Cyprus. Nur, a former ports, defense and justice minister, stressed Somalia's 15-year strategic relationship with Turkey, which last month extended the permanent presence of Turkish troops in Somalia until July 2028.
sections.whyItMatters: The episode highlights the tension in Somalia's balancing act: deepening military and economic ties with Turkey while avoiding formal recognition of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which would rupture relations with the EU and the broader international community. It also sits against Israel's December recognition of Somaliland, a rival move in the Horn of Africa.

sections.heading: Ankara Prepares New Medium-Term Economic Program
sections.body: The Turkish government plans to present its Medium-Term Economic Program for 2027-2029 in Ankara in early September, setting targets for inflation, GDP growth, unemployment, the current account balance, exports and imports, according to Azernews. Under the current program, GDP is expected to grow 3.8 percent in 2026 with an inflation target of 16 percent; authorities expect inflation to fall to 9 percent in 2027 and 8 percent in 2028. The Cabinet is also preparing the draft 2027 state budget, expected to be submitted to parliament by October 17. The program is being watched closely by international investors for signals on the lira, borrowing costs and business confidence.
sections.whyItMatters: The September unveiling will be a key test of whether Ankara holds to its disinflation path amid regional energy and oil pressures. The inflation targets — single digits by 2027 — are ambitious and will shape investor expectations for the lira and Turkish assets.

bottomLine: Today's defining development is Ankara's decision to seek an Interpol red notice for Netanyahu over the Gaza flotilla case — a legal escalation that drew a ferocious personal response from Israel and pulled Syria, Cyprus and the Kurds into the exchange. The underlying driver remains the unresolved Israel-Turkey rivalry in Syria, where Washington is pushing for a deconfliction mechanism even as Israeli strategists debate whether NATO Article 5 would shield Turkish forces. Ankara also moved on the diplomatic and economic fronts: Syria courted Pakistan within the new Makkah pact while defending Turkey's role, Somalia walked back any suggestion of recognizing northern Cyprus, and the government readied a new medium-term economic program for September. The pattern is a Turkey simultaneously escalating against Israel, consolidating its Islamic-security axis, and signaling economic continuity.
sources: France 24, Reuters, TASS, Greek City Times, The Times of Israel, Express Tribune, Cyprus Mail, Azernews, bankingnews.gr, Jerusalem Post, NYT
